name: Gratitude Journal
description: A well-studied positive psychology exercise. Writing 3 specific, detailed things you're grateful for trains your brain over time to notice more positive experiences — directly countering the negativity bias of depression.
research_basis: Emmons & McCullough (2003); Positive psychology meta-analysis; PHQ-9 mild depression protocols
tutorial_steps: Open a notebook or notes app. Write today's date.
Write 3 things you are grateful for. Be SPECIFIC — not 'my family' but 'my sister sent me a funny voice message this morning that made me smile'.
For each one, write 1 sentence about why it matters to you.
Optional: think of one person you appreciate and why.
Close the journal. It should take no more than 5 minutes.
tips: Specificity is what makes this work. Vague gratitude fades quickly; vivid, detailed appreciation sticks.
video_title: Gratitude Journaling — The Science Behind It (YouTube)

name: Light Stretching
description: Gentle movement breaks the physical stillness that reinforces depression. Even 10 minutes of light stretching increases blood flow, releases mild endorphins, and helps the body feel less stuck.
research_basis: Behavioral Activation body movement; Exercise and depression meta-analysis (Schuch, 2016)
tutorial_steps: Stand or sit on the floor. Take 3 slow breaths.
NECK: Drop right ear to right shoulder, hold 20 seconds. Repeat left.
SHOULDERS: Roll both shoulders backward 5 times, then forward 5 times.
CHEST OPENER: Clasp hands behind back, lift chest, squeeze shoulder blades gently. Hold 15 seconds.
FORWARD FOLD: Standing, slowly fold forward, letting head and arms hang. Hold 30 seconds and breathe.
SEATED TWIST: Sit cross-legged, right hand on left knee, gently twist left. Hold 20 seconds each side.
End lying flat for 1 minute, eyes closed, breathing slowly.
tips: Never stretch to the point of pain. Gentle tension you breathe into is the goal.

name: Weekly Social Activity
description: Mild depression quietly pulls people toward isolation. Scheduling one social activity weekly — however small — interrupts this before it deepens.
research_basis: Behavioral Activation social scheduling; UCLA Loneliness Scale interventions
tutorial_steps: Think of one social interaction you could have this week — coffee, a phone call, or any group activity.
Schedule it now with a specific day, time, and person.
Show up even if you don't feel like it — especially then.
After: note how you felt before vs. after on a 1-10 scale.
tips: It doesn't have to be a big event. A 20-minute coffee counts. The goal is breaking the isolation pattern.

name: Behavioral Activation Plan
description: The gold-standard behavioral treatment for depression. Depression causes withdrawal; withdrawal deepens depression. Behavioral Activation deliberately schedules small meaningful activities to break this cycle — even when motivation is absent.
research_basis: Jacobson et al. (1996); NICE depression guidelines; Dozens of RCTs
tutorial_steps: Make two lists: things that used to give you pleasure, and things that give a sense of accomplishment.
Rate each 0-10 for effort required right now.
Start with the lowest-effort items.
Schedule ONE activity for tomorrow with a specific time. (e.g., 'Walk for 10 minutes at 9 AM')
After doing it, rate mood before vs. after on 1-10.
Gradually build to 2-3 activities per day over 2 weeks.
tips: You don't need motivation to start. In depression, motivation follows action — not the other way around.

name: Connect With One Person
goals: Reactivate social bonds during mild depression
description: Depression narrows the world. This exercise makes re-connection as low-barrier as possible — one message, no expectation of a long conversation.
research_basis: Behavioral Activation social component; PHQ-9 social recovery indicators
tutorial_steps: Think of ONE person you haven't reached out to recently but care about.
Send them ONE message — as simple as: 'Hey, thinking of you. Hope you're okay.'
You don't need to share how you're feeling or have a big conversation.
Notice how you feel after sending it compared to before.
tips: Depression tells you reaching out is pointless. Do it anyway. The evidence usually proves it wrong.

name: Pleasant Activity — 15 Minutes
description: A core Behavioral Activation component. Depression suppresses the brain's reward system. Scheduling one small pleasurable activity daily begins gently restoring it.
research_basis: BAT — Behavioral Activation Therapy; Anhedonia research (Treadway & Zald, 2011)
tutorial_steps: Think of 5 activities that used to feel enjoyable OR that seem even 10% appealing right now.
Examples: one song you love, making a specific food, sitting outside, watching one episode.
Choose ONE for today. Schedule it at a specific time.
When it's time: do it, even without motivation.
After: rate 1-10 how you felt. Even 3/10 is progress.
tips: Depression lies and says nothing will feel good. Even slightly less flat counts as progress.

name: CBT Thought Record
frequency: Daily or whenever a strong negative thought occurs
description: The most researched exercise in CBT. A structured format to catch, examine, and reframe automatic negative thoughts. Used in clinical settings worldwide.
research_basis: Beck (1979) CBT for Depression; NICE guidelines; 300+ RCTs
tutorial_steps: SITUATION: What triggered the thought — where, what happened.
AUTOMATIC THOUGHT: Write the exact thought that appeared.
EMOTION: Name it and rate intensity 0-100.
EVIDENCE FOR: Facts (not feelings) that support the thought.
EVIDENCE AGAINST: Facts that challenge it. Use the 'best friend' perspective.
BALANCED THOUGHT: A realistic alternative that acknowledges both sides.
RE-RATE EMOTION: What is the intensity now? Even a 10-point drop is real progress.
tips: Ask: 'What would I tell my best friend if they had this thought?' That answer is usually your balanced thought.
video_title: How to Complete a CBT Thought Record (YouTube)

name: Behavioral Activation — Micro Steps
goals: Re-engage with daily life in tiny steps
description: For moderate depression where even small tasks feel impossible, this version breaks everything into micro-steps of 5 minutes or less — removing the activation barrier completely.
research_basis: Behavioral Activation Therapy moderate depression adaptations; Task breakdown research
tutorial_steps: Pick ONE task from your day that feels too hard.
Break it into steps so small each takes under 5 minutes. (e.g., not 'clean room' — but 'pick up 3 things from the floor')
Do only step 1. Stop there if needed. That's a real win.
Rate mood before and after step 1 and write the number down.
If energy allows, do step 2. If not — step 1 still mattered.
tips: The step should feel almost embarrassingly small. That is intentional — it bypasses the brain's resistance to starting.
video_title: Micro Steps for Depression — Getting Unstuck (YouTube)

name: Sleep Routine Checklist
description: Depression and poor sleep have a bidirectional relationship — each makes the other worse. A consistent sleep routine is a foundational intervention for moderate depression.
research_basis: CBT-I; PHQ-9 sleep item; Sleep and depression comorbidity research
tutorial_steps: Set a consistent bedtime and wake time — within 30 minutes every day including weekends.
No screens 45 minutes before bed.
Do a 5-minute body scan or breathing exercise in bed.
Keep the bedroom cool, dark, and used only for sleep.
If awake more than 20 minutes, get up and do something calm in dim light until sleepy.
Check off each habit nightly — the checklist itself becomes a routine signal.
tips: Sleep consistency is as important as sleep duration. An irregular schedule confuses the brain even if total hours are okay.

name: Daily Structure Plan
goals: Create external scaffolding when internal motivation is absent
frequency: Plan each evening for the next day
description: In moderately severe depression, the absence of structure allows hours of low mood and rumination. A simple daily schedule creates external anchors that keep the day moving even when motivation is very low.
research_basis: Behavioral Activation scheduled component; PHQ-9 severe protocol
tutorial_steps: Each evening, write tomorrow's schedule hour by hour — meals, basic hygiene, one small activity, one brief social touchpoint.
Keep expectations very low — the goal is structure, not productivity.
Morning: look at your schedule and follow it like an appointment you can't cancel.
Evening: check off what you did. Even 2 of 5 items is a real day.
tips: Structure is medicine for severe depression. It reduces the hours the brain spends in unstructured low mood.

name: Scheduled Behavioral Activation
goals: Maintain activity despite severe low mood
description: For severe depression, activities must be scheduled in advance — not chosen in the moment — because in-the-moment motivation is unavailable.
research_basis: Jacobson BA for severe depression; Pre-commitment research (Gollwitzer, 1999)
tutorial_steps: Schedule 2-3 specific activities for tomorrow NOW — not 'when you feel like it'.
Keep activities simple: a 10-min walk at 10 AM, one meal cooked at home, 5 minutes of stretching.
When the scheduled time comes: start the activity regardless of mood. Set a timer for just 5 minutes.
After 5 minutes: you may stop or continue. But the starting is the goal.
Track each activity: done / not done. Patterns emerge over a week.
tips: Pre-scheduling bypasses the depressed brain's 'I don't feel like it'. You made the decision when you were slightly more resourced.

name: Finding Professional Support
goals: Connect to professional mental health care
description: At this severity level, professional support significantly improves outcomes. This exercise helps take the concrete first step toward finding a therapist or counselor.
research_basis: NICE guidelines for moderate-severe depression and anxiety
tutorial_steps: Acknowledge: reaching out for professional help is a sign of strength.
Identify what's available to you: therapist, counselor, psychiatrist, community mental health center.
Write ONE specific action you can take today: search online, call your insurance, ask your doctor.
Do that one action today.
If cost is a barrier: look for sliding-scale therapists, community health centers, or lower-fee online platforms.
tips: You don't have to feel ready. Making the appointment is the first step — readiness often comes after.
video_title: How to Find a Therapist — Step by Step (YouTube)

name: Crisis Support Resources
description: At this severity level, professional and crisis support is essential. This provides immediate, actionable resources.
research_basis: C-SSRS crisis protocol; SAFE-T; WHO crisis guidelines
tutorial_steps: You are not alone and you deserve support right now.
Call or text a crisis line. In Egypt: 08008880700. International: findahelpline.com
Tell someone you trust how you are feeling.
If you are in immediate danger: go to the nearest emergency room or call emergency services.
Do not be alone right now if possible.
tips: Crisis lines are confidential and free. The people there are trained specifically for moments like this.
video_title: How to Use a Crisis Helpline (YouTube)

name: Personal Safety Plan
description: A written plan for what to do when distress becomes overwhelming. Evidence shows a personalized safety plan significantly reduces crisis escalation.
research_basis: Stanley & Brown Safety Planning Intervention (2012); SAFE-T protocol
tutorial_steps: WARNING SIGNS: Write feelings, thoughts, or situations that signal your distress is escalating.
INTERNAL COPING: 3 things you can do alone to reduce distress (walk, breathe, music).
SOCIAL DISTRACTION: 2-3 people or places you can go to — not to talk about crisis, just to not be alone.
TRUSTED PEOPLE: 2 people you can tell when you're really struggling.
PROFESSIONAL CONTACTS: Therapist/counselor number + a crisis line.
MEANS REDUCTION: Identify anything at home that could be dangerous; plan to reduce access.
Keep this saved on your phone's home screen or printed somewhere accessible.
tips: Build this when calmer — not during the crisis. Review it with someone you trust.
video_title: How to Make a Personal Safety Plan (YouTube)

name: Seek Immediate Professional Help
description: Severe depression requires immediate professional support. This is not a moment for self-help exercises alone.
research_basis: PHQ-9 severe depression protocol; NICE crisis pathway
tutorial_steps: Contact your doctor, therapist, or psychiatrist today — not this week, today.
If you don't have one: go to the nearest hospital or mental health center.
Tell them how long you've been feeling this way and how severe it is.
Bring a trusted person with you if possible.
You deserve and need this level of support right now.
tips: Severe depression is a medical condition. Seeking help is the most important thing you can do today.
video_title: When to Seek Help for Depression (YouTube)

name: Daily Breathing Reset
description: A foundational breathing exercise that shifts from shallow chest breathing to deep diaphragmatic breathing. Even one daily session rewires the default stress response over time.
research_basis: General anxiety maintenance; Harvard Medical School breathing research
tutorial_steps: Sit or lie down. Place one hand on your chest, one on your belly.
Breathe IN through your nose for 4 counts — the belly hand should rise, not the chest hand.
Breathe OUT through pursed lips for 6 counts, gently pressing your belly in.
Do 5-10 slow breaths.
Notice the calm that settles in your shoulders and jaw.
tips: If only your chest moves, you're not activating the diaphragm. Practice the belly rise first.

name: Light Journaling
description: Regular brief journaling externalizes anxious thoughts — moving them from the mind onto paper where they can be observed rather than experienced.
research_basis: Pennebaker expressive writing research; Anxiety self-monitoring
tutorial_steps: Open a notebook or notes app. Set a timer for 5 minutes.
Write freely — whatever is on your mind. No editing, no structure required.
When the timer ends, close the journal.
Optional: before closing, write one sentence: 'What's one thing I can do today that's in my control?'
tips: Don't re-read what you wrote. The act of writing is what clears the mental queue.

name: Daily Self-Care Checklist
description: For minimal anxiety, the goal is protection — ensuring the basics that prevent anxiety from escalating are consistently in place.
research_basis: Anxiety prevention; Lifestyle factors in GAD management
tutorial_steps: Each morning or evening, check 5 basics: sleep (7-9h?), food (ate well?), movement (some today?), water (hydrated?), one positive interaction (had one?).
If any are missing, identify the easiest way to address it tomorrow.
This is a wellbeing foundation check — not a productivity tool.
tips: Sleep, food, and movement are the three pillars that keep anxiety manageable. When all three slip, anxiety rises.

name: Box Breathing
description: Used by Navy SEALs and validated in clinical anxiety research. Four equal counts of inhale, hold, exhale, hold activate the parasympathetic nervous system rapidly.
research_basis: GAD-7 intervention; Sympathetic/parasympathetic regulation (Jerath et al., 2006)
tutorial_steps: Sit comfortably and close your eyes if possible.
Breathe IN through your nose for 4 counts.
HOLD for 4 counts.
Breathe OUT through your mouth for 4 counts.
HOLD empty for 4 counts.
Repeat for 3-5 cycles. With each round, let your shoulders drop and body soften.
tips: If 4 counts feels too long, start with 3. The hold phases activate the calming response most strongly.

name: 5-4-3-2-1 Grounding
frequency: During anxiety spikes or as needed
description: A research-backed mindfulness technique that pulls attention from anxious thoughts back into sensory experience. Effective for panic, dissociation, and thought spirals.
research_basis: MBSR grounding protocols; CBT grounding (Najavits, 2002)
tutorial_steps: Stop and take one slow breath.
Name 5 things you can SEE — be specific ('a blue plastic chair with a crack on the armrest').
Name 4 things you can FEEL physically — fabric texture, air temperature, feet on floor.
Name 3 things you can HEAR — distant sounds, near sounds, your own breathing.
Name 2 things you can SMELL (or imagine two smells you like).
Name 1 thing you can TASTE.
Take another slow breath. Has anxiety dropped at all?
tips: The more specific and vivid your observations, the better it works. The brain cannot process detailed sensory input AND anxious thoughts at the same time.

name: Gradual Exposure Ladder
goals: Face feared situations step by step
description: Avoidance maintains and grows anxiety. Gradual exposure — systematically approaching feared situations from easiest to hardest — is the most effective anxiety treatment known.
research_basis: Exposure therapy meta-analysis (Wolpe, 1958; Foa, 2011); CBT for phobias and social anxiety
tutorial_steps: Identify the situation you most avoid because of anxiety.
Build a LADDER of 8-10 steps from least scary (2/10) to most scary (10/10).
Example for social anxiety: 1) Smile at neighbor → 3) Eye contact with cashier → 5) Brief conversation → 7) Small gathering → 9) Speak up in a group.
Start at step 1. Do it. Stay until anxiety drops by at least 50%.
Repeat step 1 until it produces little anxiety. Only then move to step 2.
NEVER escape during exposure — that resets the learning.
Record anxiety before and after each step.
tips: Anxiety rising during exposure means it's working. Your willingness to feel discomfort IS the therapy. The anxiety will pass.
video_title: Exposure Therapy — How and Why It Works (YouTube)

name: Worry Time Scheduling
goals: Contain worry to a defined window
description: Instead of trying to stop worrying, you schedule a specific 15-minute daily worry window. When worries arise outside it, you postpone them. This breaks the habit of constant background worry.
research_basis: Borkovec et al. (1983) worry postponement study; GAD treatment protocols
tutorial_steps: Choose a worry time each day (e.g., 5:00-5:15 PM). NOT near bedtime.
When a worry arises outside this window, write it on a list: 'I'll think about this at 5 PM.'
At your worry window: actively think through each worry and problem-solve if you can.
After 15 minutes, close the list. Worry time is over.
If you catch yourself worrying outside the window: 'That's on my list for 5 PM.'
After one week: are your worries as urgent at 5 PM as they felt in the moment?
tips: You're not suppressing worry — you're managing it. The brain learns that worries can wait.
video_title: Worry Time — How to Stop Constant Worrying (YouTube)

name: Sleep Hygiene Checklist
description: Anxiety and poor sleep fuel each other. This checklist applies CBT-I (gold standard for insomnia) principles to break the cycle.
research_basis: CBT-I (Morin et al.); AASM Sleep Guidelines; ISI clinical protocols
tutorial_steps: Fixed wake time: same time every day — including weekends. Most important rule.
No screens 45 minutes before bed — blue light delays melatonin by 2 hours.
Bed = sleep only: no work, worry, or scrolling in bed.
Cool room: 16-19°C (60-67°F) helps trigger sleep onset.
Pre-sleep wind-down: 20 minutes of something calm before bed.
If awake 20+ minutes: get up, calm activity in dim light, return when sleepy.
tips: Start with just ONE rule this week — the most broken one. Fix it first.

name: Panic Response Plan
description: A clear step-by-step protocol for surviving a panic attack. Having a written plan transforms panic from an uncontrollable crisis into a manageable sequence.
research_basis: Panic Disorder CBT protocol (Clark, 1986)
tutorial_steps: STEP 1: Say to yourself: 'This is a panic attack. I am not in danger. It will peak in about 10 minutes and pass.'
STEP 2: Breathe IN for 5 counts, OUT for 5 counts. Repeat 10 times.
STEP 3: Plant both feet flat on the floor. Press them down firmly.
STEP 4: Name 5 things you can see around you right now.
STEP 5: Stay where you are if safe — leaving reinforces avoidance.
STEP 6: After it passes, write what triggered it if you know.
Save this as your phone lock screen so it's always accessible.
tips: Read this plan several times when CALM so your brain knows it by heart when panic hits.
video_title: What to Do During a Panic Attack (YouTube)

name: Structured Problem Solving
description: Many anxiety spirals center on real problems that feel unsolvable. Structured problem solving breaks them into manageable steps, reducing helplessness.
research_basis: Problem-Solving Therapy (PST); D'Zurilla & Goldfried (1971); CBT for GAD
tutorial_steps: Write the problem clearly in one sentence.
Brainstorm 5-8 possible solutions — no evaluation yet. Include even imperfect ones.
For each solution, rate pros and cons briefly.
Choose the best available option — not perfect, just best available.
Write the first concrete step with a specific time.
Do that step. Reassess after.
tips: Anxiety turns solvable problems into catastrophes. Writing them down and treating them as problems to solve changes everything.
